jokes.label: Joke A
jokes.title: A Convincing Performance
seedTermsUsed: Having to work with an enemy
jokes.joke: I got cast opposite my ex-wife in a romantic comedy. The director asked, 'Can you make an audience believe you're in love with her?' I said, 'I convinced her for eleven years, and she had front-row seats.'

jokes.label: Joke B
jokes.title: Method Acting
jokes.joke: My cousin is an actor, so he prepared for a role as a man losing his mind by checking into a psychiatric ward. Method acting. Three days in, he told the doctors, ‘I’m not really crazy, I’m just researching.’ They said, ‘Sure. Here’s your bracelet.’ He got the part. They got his insurance. Nobody got out.

jokes.label: Joke C
jokes.title: Small Town Nemesis
seedTermsUsed: Having to work with an enemy
jokes.joke: I grew up in a town of 400 people, which makes rivalries really inconvenient. In a city, you can just avoid your nemesis forever. But back home, my mortal enemy was also the only guy in a fifty-mile radius who could fix a broken septic tank. You haven't experienced true defeat until you're forced to smile and hand a cold lemonade to the man who ruined your life, simply because he's currently knee-deep in your family's consequences.

jokes.label: Joke D
jokes.title: Method Acting
jokes.joke: I finally booked a real acting role—as a patient in a psychiatric ward. Director said, 'Go method.' So I checked myself in. Two weeks later my agent calls: 'They love you! They're keeping you indefinitely!' I said, 'That's not a standing ovation. That's a commitment hearing.'

jokes.label: Joke E
jokes.title: Local Celebrity
jokes.joke: I moved to a tiny rural village and found out the local theater only had one actor. Every play was a one-man show. Hamlet? Same guy. The ghost? Same guy. The love interest? Still him. After intermission he walked back onstage and got a standing ovation from himself. Honestly, he deserved it for making eye contact with himself for two hours.

scores.comment: Recognizable method-acting premise, but the institutionalization twist is predictable. The insurance reference distracts, and 'Nobody got out' is a weak, unfocused closing line. More anecdote than polished stand-up.

Strong, relatable premise with a specific predicament and effective escalation. The septic-tank situation makes the rivalry amusing, and 'knee-deep in your family's consequences' delivers a clever, concrete final turn. Slightly overwritten, but genuinely funny.

Clean first-person construction, efficient setup, and a recognizable punchline. The confusion between acting success and psychiatric commitment works, although the twist is foreseeable and 'commitment hearing' is more clever than laugh-inducing.

Accessible premise with amusing possibilities, but repeating 'same guy' adds little escalation. The self-applause is predictable, and the final eye-contact observation feels arbitrary rather than delivering a strong comic reversal.

Clear stage premise and a tight turn: the 'front-row seats' reframes eleven years of marriage as a long acting job. Economical, natural first-person delivery, and the last line carries the laugh. Divorce-acting is a familiar territory, which caps originality.

Septic-tank-versus-nemesis setup is relatable and the lemonade image has promise, but it runs long and reads like an essay. The 'family's consequences' ending is a soft pun that delivers a smirk rather than a laugh, and the stage rhythm sags in the middle.

Method-acting-into-an-institution premise is clear and the standing-ovation versus commitment-hearing contrast is a real turn. The agent's 'they love you' beat is a bit predictable and the final line is slightly explained, but it is a respectable, well-built joke.

One-actor-plays-everything is an easy, readable premise and the self-ovation image is mildly funny. The closing eye-contact line is the best beat, but the list of roles is the obvious route and the escalation is flat, leaving it competent and forgettable.
Strong stage premise with a sharp, natural punchline that escalates perfectly.
Relies on a familiar trope and the final tag dilutes the rhythmic momentum.
Clean escalation with a snappy, well-crafted final line that lands the joke effectively.
Amusing imagery and competent stage rhythm, though it leans into light absurdity over a hard punch.
Clean setup and a sharp personal turn on the ex-wife; the front-row seats line lands cleanly without over-explaining.
Familiar method-acting-into-ward premise; the cousin framing and final 'nobody got out' feel forced rather than earned.
Specific, grounded rural-enemy image builds well to the lemonade-and-septic payoff; the 'family's consequences' turn is sharp and human.
Cute one-man-show escalation with a solid self-ovation closer, but the laugh stays mild rather than explosive.
Clear first-person setup and strong closing line; familiar ex-spouse misdirection but effective.
Not first-person stand-up; largely a familiar method-acting-in-psychiatric-ward premise with an overstretched ending.
Specific rural image and solid escalation; more amusing than laugh-out-loud, but well constructed.
Clean first-person structure and tidy commitment-hearing punchline; familiar premise executed competently.
